claim: GJP training and teaming effects on forecast skill are contested: a 2025 IRT reanalysis found they vanish, shrink or reverse once extraneous variables are controlled.
note: Reanalysis uses the same GJP data as Mellers 2014 (one dissent, not a replication). Do not build on 'training works' as proven.

claim: Traits tied to strategic responding separate superforecasters, so the cause of their edge is hard to identify.
note: One reanalysis, fetched three times. Weakens the 'superforecaster habits cause skill' story.

claim: Extremizing an aggregate helps only when forecasters hold diverse private information; the best amount depends on information overlap.
note: One theory paper (cite arXiv 1406.2148; 1501.06943 withdrawn). a-09 (Satopaa 2021, snippet) says noise removal mattered more than bias correction. Implication that one-model samples should not be extremized is our inference, untested.

claim: Superforecaster edge figures (35-72% better, 30% over analysts) are promotional or press claims, not peer-reviewed effect sizes.
note: Both via Wikipedia. Use only as a warning.

claim: Cognitive ability, knowledge and open-mindedness predict forecast accuracy.
note: Snippet only, not confirmed by fetch.

claim: People are overconfident: stated certainty and 90% intervals exceed hit rates; the planning fallacy shows inside-view estimates run too optimistic, which motivates reference-class use.
note: Classic human studies (Buehler 1994 n=37, Lichtenstein 1982 review); a-13 is Wikipedia. Human data, transfer to LLMs by analogy only.

claim: LLMs verbalising confidence are overconfident; larger models calibrate better; no elicitation technique wins consistently; all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
note: One study (Xiong 2024) fetched three times. Mei 2025 and Tian 2023 support overconfidence but are different claims.

claim: Consistency across sampled responses and better aggregation reduce verbalised overconfidence.
note: Xiong 2024 and Kuhn 2023 are independent. Caveat: same-model samples are correlated, and gains are over a weak baseline.

claim: For RLHF models, verbalised confidence beats token probabilities, roughly halving calibration error on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA.
note: One study, three benchmarks, weak baseline.

claim: Large models are reasonably calibrated on multiple choice and true/false in the right format; self-evaluation (P(True)) improves when the model sees several of its own samples; P(IK) generalises poorly.
note: One preprint (Kadavath 2022), format-dependent, older models.

claim: Grouping sampled answers by meaning (semantic entropy) predicts QA accuracy better than comparable baselines without model changes.
note: Kuhn 2023 only. Farquhar 2024 from the earlier brief was not fetched. QA tasks only.

claim: Reasoning-model calibration: better than non-reasoning in 33 of 36 settings and improving along the chain, versus overconfident (over 85% when wrong), worse with depth, introspection hurt Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and fewer 'I don't know' answers.
note: Three independent preprints (Yoon, Mei, Zeng). Yoon and Mei conflict directly; the split may be by task type and model. All preprints.

claim: LLM forecasting systems with retrieval and ensembling approach the human crowd, but experts and superforecasters still lead on ForecastBench (about 0.017 Brier; parity projected near late 2026).
note: Halawi 2024, Karger 2025, FRI update, Alur 2025, Lu 2025. Mostly preprints; a-22 is an organisation page. AIA parity claim (preprint) is in mild tension with expert-lead results.

claim: A crowd of 12 LLMs matched 925 humans on 31 questions with a yes-bias; showing the human median helped weaker models but plain averaging beat it.
note: One small study (31 questions). Suggestive only.

claim: LLM forecasts are logically inconsistent across related questions, and the inconsistency score correlates with later Brier score.
note: One preprint (Paleka 2025). Usable as a label-free check.

claim: Pastcasting on resolved questions gives results comparable to live forecasting; leaked-answer retrodiction inflates scores.
note: b-11 is abstract only; c-13 is a benchmark design note. Weak link.

claim: Outcome-based RL on forecasting improved a 14B model's calibration and matched o1 accuracy.
note: Abstract-only preprint.

claim: In LLM agents, step-level calibration does not imply trajectory-level calibration; step errors are coupled and averaging hides late overconfidence.
note: One 2026 preprint, 4 models.

claim: Experts' long-run political predictions were often no better than simple baselines; foxes beat hedgehogs.
note: Memory only; no number verified.

claim: A forecasting procedure needs a gate on single-answer tasks, since forced extra steps hurt in our own measurements; no source tests forecasting procedures on LLMs at equal tokens.
note: Our project data plus absence of evidence; not external.
